title: From One Day to One Year

scenes.tts: How can a tree or butterfly act on time without a calendar? Watch one dial carry a day inside a year. Its blue light band turns. Its red temperature band rises and falls. The living things change with it.
scenes.caption: How can a tree or butterfly act on time without a calendar? Watch one dial carry a day inside a year. Its blue light band turns. Its red temperature band rises and falls. The living things change with it.
scenes.visual: COLOR MAP for both films: light and day length BLUE; temperature RED; inner rhythm GOLD; response GREEN. Fill the frame with a circular year dial. A smaller day-night dial turns inside it. Blue daylight sweeps across the inner dial while a red seasonal arc slowly rises and falls outside. A cherry twig, monarch and groundhog sit around the rim and subtly move.
scenes.narration: How can a tree or butterfly act on time without a calendar? Watch one dial carry a day inside a year. Its blue light band turns. Its red temperature band rises and falls. The living things change with it.

scenes.visual: Brief title over the still-turning nested dial: From One Day to One Year. Keep both dials moving behind the title.

scenes.tts: Start with the inner dial. A circadian rhythm repeats about once each day. Light and darkness help keep many rhythms aligned. Many owls and many bats hunt at night. Tree squirrels and most songbirds are active by day. Yet the rhythm is not simply a reaction to each sunrise.
scenes.caption: Start with the inner dial. A circadian rhythm repeats about once each day. Light and darkness help keep many rhythms aligned. Many owls and many bats hunt at night. Tree squirrels and most songbirds are active by day. Yet the rhythm is not simply a reaction to each sunrise.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the inner dial. Show a gold activity wave circling beneath the blue day-night band. Label the blue band LIGHT AND DARK and the gold wave INNER RHYTHM. Put 24 h on the dial without narrating it. An owl rises on the dark half while a squirrel rises on the light half.
scenes.narration: Start with the inner dial. A circadian rhythm repeats about once each day. Light and darkness help keep many rhythms aligned. Many owls and many bats hunt at night. Tree squirrels and most songbirds are active by day. Yet the rhythm is not simply a reaction to each sunrise.

scenes.tts: Here is your prediction. The blue light band disappears, leaving steady darkness. Will the gold activity rhythm vanish at once, or keep circling for a while? Watch the gold marker carefully. Choose before the dial moves.
scenes.caption: Here is your prediction. The blue light band disappears, leaving steady darkness. Will the gold activity rhythm vanish at once, or keep circling for a while? Watch the gold marker carefully. Choose before the dial moves.
scenes.visual: Fade the blue band to black but leave the gold wave poised on the dial. Large question: VANISH OR CONTINUE? The owl and squirrel freeze in neutral poses. A small gold marker pulses gently.
scenes.narration: Here is your prediction. The blue light band disappears, leaving steady darkness. Will the gold activity rhythm vanish at once, or keep circling for a while? Watch the gold marker carefully. Choose before the dial moves.

scenes.visual: Hold VANISH OR CONTINUE? Keep the gold marker pulsing and a thin thinking ring expanding slowly. No other answer cue appears.

scenes.tts: In many animals, it keeps circling for a while. That tells us some timing comes from inside the body. Outside light still matters because it keeps that inner rhythm lined up with the day. Inner timing and outside light work together.
scenes.caption: In many animals, it keeps circling for a while. That tells us some timing comes from inside the body. Outside light still matters because it keeps that inner rhythm lined up with the day. Inner timing and outside light work together.
scenes.visual: Animate the gold wave completing another circuit in darkness. Then restore the blue band slightly ahead of the gold peak. Slide the gold wave into alignment with blue and label the motion KEPT IN STEP.
scenes.narration: In many animals, it keeps circling for a while. That tells us some timing comes from inside the body. Outside light still matters because it keeps that inner rhythm lined up with the day. Inner timing and outside light work together.

scenes.tts: Not every response is a rhythm. A tropism is plant growth toward or away from something. Light moves beside a bean shoot. Cells lengthen more on the shaded side, so new growth bends toward light. Roots can also curve toward wetter places.
scenes.caption: Not every response is a rhythm. A tropism is plant growth toward or away from something. Light moves beside a bean shoot. Cells lengthen more on the shaded side, so new growth bends toward light. Roots can also curve toward wetter places.
scenes.visual: Transform the inner dial into a large bean shoot. A blue lamp glides to the left. Show two labelled blocks across the stem: SHADED SIDE stretches taller in GREEN while LIT SIDE stays shorter. The shoot curves toward the lamp. Mark the drawing SCHEMATIC.
scenes.narration: Not every response is a rhythm. A tropism is plant growth toward or away from something. Light moves beside a bean shoot. Cells lengthen more on the shaded side, so new growth bends toward light. Roots can also curve toward wetter places.

scenes.tts: Now widen back to the year. Shorter days and cooler air can time seasonal responses. Monarchs migrate. Tree buds become dormant. Groundhogs hibernate, lowering body temperature and using less stored energy. Deciduous trees also drop leaves as winter approaches.
scenes.caption: Now widen back to the year. Shorter days and cooler air can time seasonal responses. Monarchs migrate. Tree buds become dormant. Groundhogs hibernate, lowering body temperature and using less stored energy. Deciduous trees also drop leaves as winter approaches.
scenes.visual: Return to the outer dial. The blue day-length arc shrinks toward fall while the red temperature arc falls. A GREEN monarch marker travels south, a GREEN bud closes, and a GREEN groundhog temperature bar drops. Keep all responses attached to the same turning dial.
scenes.narration: Now widen back to the year. Shorter days and cooler air can time seasonal responses. Monarchs migrate. Tree buds become dormant. Groundhogs hibernate, lowering body temperature and using less stored energy. Deciduous trees also drop leaves as winter approaches.

scenes.tts: These responses meet a hard season in different ways. Migration changes place. Dormancy slows growth while life continues. Hibernation is animal dormancy, not one unbroken sleep. Groundhogs briefly warm, then cool again. Each response helps the organism meet hard conditions.
scenes.caption: These responses meet a hard season in different ways. Migration changes place. Dormancy slows growth while life continues. Hibernation is animal dormancy, not one unbroken sleep. Groundhogs briefly warm, then cool again. Each response helps the organism meet hard conditions.
scenes.visual: Follow each response around one shared winter sector. The monarch crosses a map arrow. The closed bud shows a tiny steady GREEN life pulse. The groundhog temperature bar makes a short rise, then falls. Labels transform in place: MOVE, PAUSE GROWTH, COOL AND REWARM.
scenes.narration: These responses meet a hard season in different ways. Migration changes place. Dormancy slows growth while life continues. Hibernation is animal dormancy, not one unbroken sleep. Groundhogs briefly warm, then cool again. Each response helps the organism meet hard conditions.

scenes.tts: Outside cues are not the whole story. Some animals also have inner yearly timing. With day length held steady, groundhog eating and weight cycles kept repeating about once a year. Many seasonal behaviors are inherited. A first-time monarch can fly south without being taught, although some animals do learn routes.
scenes.caption: Outside cues are not the whole story. Some animals also have inner yearly timing. With day length held steady, groundhog eating and weight cycles kept repeating about once a year. Many seasonal behaviors are inherited. A first-time monarch can fly south without being taught, although some animals do learn routes.
scenes.visual: Add a slow GOLD ring inside the seasonal dial and label it INNER YEARLY TIMING. A young monarch follows a GREEN south arrow without an older butterfly. Then a small separate pair of birds travels together under the label SOME ROUTES ARE LEARNED.
scenes.narration: Outside cues are not the whole story. Some animals also have inner yearly timing. With day length held steady, groundhog eating and weight cycles kept repeating about once a year. Many seasonal behaviors are inherited. A first-time monarch can fly south without being taught, although some animals do learn routes.

scenes.tts: Species combine cues differently. Many tree buds need winter cold before later warmth can open them. The order of cues can matter. So one warm day is not a universal start button. The response depends on the organism's timing system.
scenes.caption: Species combine cues differently. Many tree buds need winter cold before later warmth can open them. The order of cues can matter. So one warm day is not a universal start button. The response depends on the organism's timing system.
scenes.visual: On the same dial, move a bud through a blue COLD sector before the red WARM sector. Only after both sectors pass does the bud open GREEN. Beside it, a second schematic bud skips cold and remains closed with a question mark, not a claim of failure.
scenes.narration: Species combine cues differently. Many tree buds need winter cold before later warmth can open them. The order of cues can matter. So one warm day is not a universal start button. The response depends on the organism's timing system.

scenes.tts: The picture now has two kinds of timing. Gold inner rhythms keep turning. Blue and red cues help line up responses with the world. No single cue controls every organism. Across days and seasons, the useful response arrives at a useful time.
scenes.caption: The picture now has two kinds of timing. Gold inner rhythms keep turning. Blue and red cues help line up responses with the world. No single cue controls every organism. Across days and seasons, the useful response arrives at a useful time.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the full nested dial. Gold inner rings turn, blue and red cue bands sweep, and green response markers align. Use arrows only from the cue bands and inner rings toward the response markers. Keep the motion continuous.
scenes.narration: The picture now has two kinds of timing. Gold inner rhythms keep turning. Blue and red cues help line up responses with the world. No single cue controls every organism. Across days and seasons, the useful response arrives at a useful time.

scenes.visual: Clear everything to one centered line only: 'Inner rhythms and environmental cues time responses; long-term changes can shift them.'
